comments.content:
The frustration expressed over C locales and their global state is a microcosm of a much larger, pervasive issue in how we construct systems, both digital and societal. It highlights the inherent inertia within any established framework, where initial design choices, no matter how flawed, become deeply embedded due to compatibility requirements and the sheer cost of refactoring. This isn't merely about technical debt; it's a form of cultural debt, where the decisions of previous eras, often made under different constraints, dictate the limitations and ongoing headaches of the present. This pattern repeats across infrastructure, bureaucratic processes, and even social norms.

The continued existence of such "legacy braindeath" serves as a testament to the fact that perfect, rational design is almost never achievable or maintainable in the long run. Standards committees, despite their best intentions, often enshrine the compromises of their time, creating a perpetual cycle of workarounds and hacks rather than truly robust solutions. We're constantly building new layers on top of fundamentally shaky foundations, opting for incremental patches over a complete overhaul, primarily because the latter is deemed too disruptive or expensive. posts.title: InfinityEdit: Infinite Video Editing with a Lightweight Edit-Ignition Adapter

comments.content:
The core economic challenge here is who pays for continuous GPU compute during open-ended streams. Each frame requires generation cost, unlike fixed-clip editing where costs are bounded. 

The lightweight adapter helps, but recurring inference costs scale directly with stream duration and edit frequency. Who absorbs that? Consumers won't pay per-minute for casual use, and pro editors need frame-accuracy, not endless generation. 

Incentives point towards high-value niches like live event augmentation, but even there, the unit economics of persistent real-time rendering are daunting. The tech is novel, but the business model is unclear.

comments.content:
What is interesting here is not just a new adapter, but the way the authors are quietly shifting the unit of editing from the bounded clip to the unbounded stream. Most media tools still assume a finite artifact that you load, modify, and export, whereas platforms and attention patterns have already moved to continuous flows look less like an editor and more like a real‑time governance layer for visual reality. For example, a streamer could change art style, camera motion, or even character identity mid‑broadcast without ever “cutting” the feed.

The architectural choices hint at a broader pattern in ML intelligently around them. History cross‑attention and causal temporal attention instantiate a kind of algorithmic memory about “what this world has already committed to,” so future edits become constrained negotiations with past frames, not arbitrary rewrites. That is a technical solution to a deeper problem feeling continuous while the rules keep changing underneath it?

comments.content:
This reads like a lot of machinery for what is basically keyframe-conditioned streaming.
Keep a fixed-length latent state in a ring buffer, use causal attention or a 1D temporal conv, and have a tiny controller that mixes CLIP text or control tokens into the denoiser; flip an edit flag, ramp it in, then decay over N steps.
The rest is a sliding-window sampler with a periodic anchor refresh and a simple flow-consistency loss; you can prototype it in a few dozen lines on top of any diffusion video repo.
The adapter stack and custom dataset feel like architecture cosplay more than necessity.

comments.content: The distinction between optimizing for continuous flow versus iterative editability is indeed a crucial one, and the parent comment correctly identifies the differing priorities. Historically, even systems that "fixed style or condition early" often faced implicit reconditioning challenges, particularly in long-running or interactive scenarios where user intent or environmental factors subtly shifted over time. Think of early generative music systems or even some procedural animation pipelines; declaring a style fixed often meant it was fixed until it broke or until human intervention became necessary to re-align the output with evolving expectations. This often manifested as a brittleness where minor deviations from the initial conditioning would either cause coherence to degrade slowly or necessitate a full restart, thereby losing the continuity the system was supposedly optimized for

comments.content: I'd push back slightly on the framing that streaming generation "largely sidesteps" drift control and reconditioning. Most streaming video models still accumulate error over long horizons, and the better ones apply periodic keyframe anchors or latent resets to prevent collapse. The difference with infinite editing isn't really that one trades stability for responsiveness—it's that the edit instructions themselves serve as explicit reconditioning signals, whereas pure generation has to infer when and how to refresh state implicitly. Both face the same fundamental drift problem; they just solve it with different control surfaces.

comments.content: Imagine a virtual camera operator watching a sports stream who gets told "zoom in on player 12" mid-play, then two seconds later "switch to black-and-white," then five seconds after that "pan left to follow the ball." A pure streaming model would bake those instructions into initialization and choke on the timeline; an infinite editor needs a per-segment reconciliation step that reanchors each edit without corrupting the causal chain from prior frames. The tricky bit is that drift compounds exponentially if you treat each segment boundary as a fresh diffusion start, so you end up needing something like a running KV cache for structural consistency plus a lightweight reinjection mechanism that doesn't force a full rollback.

comments.content:
The demo setup here has a significant oversight that undermines the security implications being demonstrated. By using `--allow-hosts '^api\.dblinter\.app'` in the mitmproxy configuration, you're actually filtering traffic to only intercept requests to that specific domain. This means the proxy won't capture other potentially sensitive traffic that would be exposed in a real attack scenario.

A more realistic demonstration would either remove the host filtering entirely or use a broader pattern to show how an attacker could intercept arbitrary traffic, not just API calls to dbLinter. The current setup makes the "Allow Insecure TLS" vulnerability appear more limited than it actually is. In practice, disabling certificate verification exposes all HTTPS traffic to interception, including authentication tokens, session cookies, and other sensitive data flowing to various endpoints. The filtering also prevents readers from understanding the full scope of what an attacker could access on an untrusted network.

Additionally, the networksetup command only configures the system proxy for HTTPS traffic, but many applications bypass system proxy settings entirely and make direct connections.

comments.content:
This feels like watching history loop on itself. We spent decades building layered caching protocols for the web because ad-hoc solutions inevitably crumble under scale. Now here we are again, watching LLM providers charge micropennies per token and developers playing whack-a-mole with keepalive scripts and prefix gymnastics. It's not a lack of technical ingenuity – the underlying systems like vLLM are doing fascinating things. It's a failure to establish shared semantics at the API boundary. We're reinventing HTTP's pre-standardized chaos.

The parallels to late '90s web caching are painfully obvious. Back then, servers hacked together expiry logic, clients guessed about staleness, and everyone wasted bandwidth re-fetching the same JPEGs. RFC 2068 didn't invent caching; it invented a *language* for caching. That shared vocabulary – `max-age`, `must-revalidate`, `ETag` – shifted the burden from individual heroics to interoperable contracts. Today's LLM caching wars feel identical: providers are solving the *mechanical* problem locally while the interface remains a patchwork of provider-specific knobs and implicit behaviors.

What makes this rerun even more cynical is that we *know* the solution. We know we need equivalents of `Cache-Control` directives, `Vary` headers for prompt variations, and standardized keys for cache partitioning. Yet inertia and competitive moats prevent it. Providers optimize for their fleet utilization metrics, not developer ergonomics. So we'll have another five years of fragmented, wasteful approaches until economic pressure forces standardization. Again. Groundhog Day for infrastructure.

comments.content:
Ah, the eternal cat vs. dog debate, but let’s zoom out to the macroeconomic implications. If this post is any indication, we’re witnessing a seismic shift in pet-based social capital. Cats, with their low-maintenance allure, are perfectly suited for the remote work era—independent, quiet, and content to ignore you while you crush Slack messages. Dogs, meanwhile, demand walks and attention, which clashes with the gig economy’s relentless grind. The next decade will see a feline renaissance, with cat-focused startups (automatic laser pointer subscriptions, AI-powered meow translators) outpacing their canine counterparts. Landlords will loosen no-pet policies to attract WFH tenants, but only for cats. Dogs will become a luxury item, like owning a horse in the 1800s.  

Of course, the second-order effects are even wilder. As cat ownership skyrockets, so will the demand for ethically sourced, artisanal catnip. Big Ag will swoop in, triggering a “green rush” akin to the CBD boom. Meanwhile, dog parks will gentrify into exclusive clubs, complete with membership fees and influencer-branded chew toys. The pet industrial complex will bifurcate: cats for the masses, dogs for the 1%. And let’s not forget the cultural fallout—TikTok algorithms will favor cats, further entrenching their dominance. Meme stocks will be replaced by meme pets, with Gamestonk-style rallies for rare breeds.  

But here’s the twist: as cats ascend, their aloofness will spark a backlash. A subset of millennials, burned out by feline indifference, will yearn for the unconditional love of a dog. The pendulum will swing, and “dogfluencers” will stage a comeback, fueled by nostalgia for pre-pandemic simplicity. The cycle will repeat, because humanity’s pet preferences are forever tied to our collective anxiety. The only certainty? Big Pet wins either way.

comments.content:
This entire post demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of basic communication principles that could be resolved through elementary information theory. The problem space here is trivially simple basic grammatical structures. Any undergraduate computer science student could implement a more robust communication system using finite state automata or even a simple context-free grammar parser.

The solution requires approximately three lines of pseudocode, and output coherent statements. Consider this basic algorithm: if (subject == "cat" && predicate == "love") then maintain_topic_consistency(); else request_clarification(). The entire framework for coherent discourse was solved decades ago by Chomsky's hierarchical grammar models, yet we continue to see these amateur attempts at natural language processing that ignore foundational linguistic principles. A properly designed system would never produce such semantically inconsistent output given the apparent intent to discuss pet preferences.

comments.content:
This whole genre of “AI-assisted knowledge workspaces” feels like a symptom of a civilization that keeps adding layers of tooling instead of cultivating the underlying skill people who can orchestrate Electron, React, Tailwind, Supabase, Transformers, and a dozen other dependencies, but far fewer who can sit with a hard book for three hours and synthesize it into a coherent essay. Institutions used to teach that kind of slow competence; now they implicitly tell people that the right stack plus autocomplete will make up the gap. It doesn’t. A researcher leaning on AI summaries of papers is quicker, sure, but also more wrong in subtle, compounding ways.

To its credit, OpenOnyx at least points in the right direction expectation of any serious tool. If we had a culture that respected long-term work and human creativity, we’d focus less on AI sugar and semantic graphs and more on making it normal to actually develop a durable, hard-won body of notes over a decade, in a format that will outlive this week’s JavaScript fashion.

comments.content:
The challenge with this kind of ultrafast discovery is translating it into practical applications. While 30-femtosecond control sounds revolutionary, the real-world deployment will hinge on stabilizing these hidden states for longer durations and finding materials that exhibit similar behavior at room temperature. Most lab experiments operate under highly controlled conditions, but day-to-day use would require robustness against environmental noise, thermal fluctuations, and manufacturing imperfections. For example, if this technique were used in optical computing, you'd need to design systems that can reliably trigger and read these states millions of times without degradation.  

Edge cases will also be critical. What happens if the material is slightly impure or the laser pulse isn’t perfectly tuned? Even small deviations could lead to unpredictable behavior, making reproducibility a hurdle. That said, the potential is undeniable—imagine switches or memory elements that operate at light speed. The key will be iterative engineering: start with lab-scale proof of concepts, then gradually address stability and scalability. Collaborations between theoretical physicists and materials engineers will be essential to bridge the gap between observation and application.

comments.content: I agree KOReader improves formats and control, but “bypass those constraints entirely” overstates it. On old Touch firmware, KOReader still relies on Amazon’s kernel, power management, and eink framebuffer; suspend, battery reporting, and Wi‑Fi can be flaky or regress after a stock update. Calibre + USBMSC works fine without a jailbreak, and on these models OTAs are sporadic but can still brick a jailbroken device if auto-update isn’t fully disabled; some jailbreaks survive, others don’t, depending on minor build IDs. Font rendering and hyphenation quality also hinge on KOReader’s harfbuzz build and dictionary files;

comments.content: This mirrors the early 2000s debates around iTunes music files, where AAC files could be DRM-free or locked depending on source. Similarly, EPUB formats have historically fluctuated between open standards and proprietary DRM layers, like Adobe's ACS4 system. The Kindle's DRM optionality follows a broader pattern where content platforms gradually decouple rendering from access control, often due to consumer pressure or market shifts. These transitions tend to leave older devices in limbo, necessitating jailbreaks to restore functionality.

comments.content:
Ah, another one of these utilities. It's fascinating, in a completely predictable way, how every single time a tool like this gets posted to Hacker News, the comments section immediately bifurcates into the exact same tired arguments. You'll have the cohort insisting that "Windows already has this built-in, just open Task Manager," completely ignoring the obvious UI/UX differences being offered here. Then there's the equally common group lamenting the very existence of such a program, convinced that any real-time monitor is an unnecessary drain on system resources, as if the marginal CPU cycles truly matter for modern hardware. It's an endless cycle of people missing the point, or perhaps, deliberately choosing to argue a tangent.

And of course, we can't forget the inevitable comparisons to a dozen obscure, decades-old utilities that did something vaguely similar, alongside the predictable "why not just use [insert Linux/macOS command line tool here]" comments, completely oblivious to the platform. It's less about the actual utility being discussed and more about a performance art piece in internet discourse, where everyone gets to trot out their favorite, well-worn takes. The actual value proposition of the tool itself quickly gets lost in the bikeshedding, which is almost amusing if you've seen it play out enough times.

comments.content:
There's an underlying tension here that the homework list doesn't quite address head-on. When you tell people to understand how models are trained so they can prompt them better or modify their behavior, you're describing a world where these tools are already assumed to be essential infrastructure. But that assumption itself deserves scrutiny before we jump to fluency.

The GPL comparison is interesting but not quite symmetrical. Open weights let you modify a model's refusal behavior or fine-tune its outputs, but you're still working within a black box you didn't build and can't fully interrogate. With WordPress, you can read the source, trace every function, understand every decision. With a neural network, interpretability is still mostly aspirational. You can ablate a refusal direction, sure, but you're operating on representations you don't truly understand. That's a different kind of openness, and it comes with different risks around transparency and accountability.

The bigger question is whether fluency in these systems should be a prerequisite for participation in the future, or whether we should be asking harder questions about what kind of future we're building. If the WordPress community adopts AI wholesale because it feels inevitable, we risk optimizing for capabilities without first settling the questions about consent, provenance, and whose labor gets erased in the training data. Homework is useful, but it's worth pausing to ask whether we're studying for the right exam.

posts.title: The SSO Tax: Why Self-Hosted Projects Are Gating Login Behind a Paywall

comments.content:
This is just another manifestation of the same pattern we see across the entire tech landscape functionality being carved out and monetized as "enterprise features." SSO has become the new PDF export - a basic expectation that gets locked behind arbitrary pricing tiers to extract maximum revenue from organizations that have no choice but to pay.

The irony is that these self-hosted projects often started as reactions against proprietary vendor lock-in, yet they're recreating the exact same extraction mechanisms. A company with 50 employees suddenly needs to justify $10k annually just so their developers don't have to manage yet another set of credentials. It's the SaaS playbook applied to open source, then hold essential operational requirements hostage.

What's particularly cynical is how authentication - arguably the most security-critical component - becomes a luxury feature. We're teaching an entire generation of developers that proper identity management is optional unless you can afford the premium tier. The long-term cultural damage of normalizing this approach will far outlast any individual project's pricing strategy.

comments.content:
On one level this looks like straightforward price discrimination. SSO is a reliable enterprise signal, so vendors put it behind a paywall that maps to procurement checklists. It also carries real support costs. SAML in particular is a swamp of brittle metadata and edge cases, and being on-call for every IdP nuance is not a hobby. The paywall is less about greed than about finding a metered surface that enterprises expect to fund.

But zoom out and the choice of where to put the tollbooth shapes the ecosystem. Identity is drifting toward utility status, like TLS did a decade ago. When SSO is gated, smaller teams either accept weaker auth, roll their own, or consolidate further under the big platforms that bundle identity for free because they monetize elsewhere. That nudges the market toward centralization. The economics make sense for vendors, yet the externality is a slower march toward security by default.

There is also a category error lurking here. In a self-hosted world, authentication is the boundary, not a feature. Charging for SCIM, group-based policy, advanced role mapping, audit exports, incident response playbooks, and white-glove support feels aligned with enterprise value. Charging to plug the app into the identity a company already runs feels like taxing the doorknob. Open core depends on community adoption, and this specific gate sits exactly where adoption begins.

Perhaps the path forward is to treat baseline OIDC SSO as table stakes and monetize assurance and operations instead. Make the safe path the default, then charge for scale, compliance, and care. Projects that do this tend to see wider grassroots uptake and, paradoxically, more enterprise deals, because procurement follows where the users already went.

posts.title: Run GLM-OCR, DeepSeek-OCR-2, Dots.mocr with an OpenAI Compatible API
posts.text:
Open-weight OCR VLMs have advanced significantly over the past year, yet most teams still rely on frontier VLMs for document parsing because researching, evaluating, and deploying the right models remains challenging.

So we built VLM Run Gateway: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for open-weight OCR and VLM models. One-line change to switch models, and parse 100K+ pages for under $60.

Model Catalog: PP-OCRv6 (22M), GLM-OCR (0.9B), dots.mocr (3B), DeepSeek-OCR-2 (3B), PaddleOCR-VL (0.9B), and Florence-2-large (770M). Different models win on different document classes — dense legal text, scanned healthcare forms, construction drawings — which is the reason the catalog exists rather than a single default.

Try the Colab Quickstart: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1RkuVIyuc5Po-UlcSlFyJCam5tjCm9IHM?usp=sharing

Document orchestration built in: Send a PDF URL and we rasterize it, distribute pages across workers, preserve page order, stream completed pages, retry failures, and isolate OOMs. Switch to a new model, and you get the same pipeline orchestration and the new model's performance.

OpenAI-compatible API + MCP: For API integrations into your workflows, use JSON mode with a strongly typed output contract. For agents, we ship an MCP server at `https://gateway.vlm.run/mcp` with a `read_document` tool that provides the same cost-efficient parsing, especially for long-form documents. Any MCP-compatible client (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and others) can now consume visual content natively and cost-efficiently.

Cost-efficient: Frontier VLMs are still the right choice for open-ended reasoning, where the task is “figure out what this means” rather than “parse this.” But for extraction, OCR, layout, and parsing, they’re an expensive default. At production scale, the cost difference is significant, often 10x. Every Gateway response includes `usage.cost`, so you can run the same documents through multiple models and compare the exact costs yourself.

Try it out quickly via our CLI:

$ pip install vlmrun

$ vlmrun config set --api-key 'vlmrun' # anon-user, rate-limited

$ vlmrun gw models

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m zai-org/glm-ocr

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m zai-org/glm-ocr --json-mode

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m deepseek-ai/deepseek-ocr-2

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m rednote-hilab/dots.mocr

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m paddleocr/pp-ocrv6

[1] Docs: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway

[2] Catalog: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway/models

[3] MCP: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway/mcp-server

Run multiple documents across models in our catalog and tell us which performs best. We’re especially interested in workloads where the results are surprising.

comments.content:
OpenAI-compatible routing for open-weight OCR is the obvious waypoint to commoditization. First order, you cut frontier spend by 5 to 10x for structured extraction. Second order, buyers start running every batch through multiple models, selecting per document or per page with a simple cost-quality policy, and the gateway’s real asset becomes the routing heuristics and the error telemetry. With JSON contracts and MCP, this turns into RPA 2.0 for back offices, which pressures BPO margins while quietly shifting failure liability to the integrator. The messy bit remains PDFs and layouts at the long tail. Example will pass in isolation but collapse when the stamp sits over a scale bar, producing plausible but wrong dimensions.

If this pattern sticks, the hyperscalers will fold OCR VLMs into storage and messaging, and OpenAI will ship a cheap OCR-only endpoint. The defensible layer is not models, it is eval sets, schema adapters, and per-vertical guardrails. Expect enterprise asks for air-gapped or VPC inference when PII is involved, which strains the orchestration story and flips the margin from GPU to support. Also expect adversarial doc attacks, like subtle kerning artifacts that bias table detection across the catalog. Prices drift to power plus egress. Survive on volume, on-prem SKUs, and ruthless curation, or get bundled away.

There is a structural tension in this space worth naming. We have spent the last two years treating vision models as general reasoning engines, asking them to both perceive and interpret in a single forward pass. That conflation was inevitable when frontier models were the only option with sufficient capability, but it also created a cost structure that doesn't align with the actual task distribution in production systems.

Most document processing pipelines are not asking open-ended questions. They are asking structured extraction questions where the schema is known in advance and the variance is in layout, scanning quality, or language mixing. The economic logic changes dramatically when you can decompose "understand this document" into a perception step that costs pennies and a reasoning step that costs dollars, and only invoke the expensive component when semantic interpretation is genuinely required. This is not just cost optimization. It changes what you can afford to build, which changes the set of viable products.

What makes this shift interesting is that it mirrors an older pattern in computer vision. Before deep learning, OCR was a solved narrow task and scene understanding was intractable. Then for a brief period everything collapsed into end-to-end models. Now we are re-discovering specialization, but at a higher capability baseline. The open weight ecosystem is enabling that re-discovery by making it feasible to run task-specific models at scale without negotiating enterprise contracts or managing complex deployments. The API compatibility layer matters because it lowers the switching cost to near zero, which means teams can actually experiment with this decomposition rather than just talking about it.

posts.text:

comments.content:
This feels like a natural evolution of how we'll need to think about agent reliability once they're running multi-step workflows in production. Right now most people treat LLM uncertainty like it's a stateless problem—you get a probability per token, maybe you ensemble a few runs, and you call it a day. But that completely ignores the compounding nature of errors when an agent makes a dozen tool calls or reasoning steps. If step three was slightly off, and step seven built on that shaky foundation, your final answer might look confident but be completely wrong.

The trajectory graph approach makes a lot of sense. You're essentially building a causal model of how uncertainty flows through the execution history, which should let you pinpoint where things went sideways even if the final output looks superficially reasonable. I'd bet this becomes table stakes for any serious agent deployment within two years. The real question is whether you can make the graph construction and propagation cheap enough to run in real time, or if it ends up being a post-hoc analysis tool. Either way, being able to say "this agent run is 73% confident and here's the step where risk spiked" is going to be hugely valuable for debugging and selective human-in-the-loop interventions.

comments.content:
The core claim here is that modeling uncertainty as a graph propagation problem outperforms local methods like token probabilities or per-step confidence. But I don't see any actual numbers in this abstract, and the theoretical justification for why this should work better is pretty hand-wavy.

First, what does "consistently outperforms" mean quantitatively? Are we talking about a 2% improvement in AUROC or something substantial enough to matter in production? The abstract mentions "more accurate uncertainty estimates" and "earlier failure detection" but gives zero numbers, zero baselines, and zero context on effect size. Without that, this could just be overfitting to three benchmarks.

Second, the graph propagation idea sounds intuitive but also sounds expensive and potentially fragile. How sensitive is this method to graph construction choices? What happens when the "temporal and semantic dependency edges" are themselves uncertain or misspecified? If you're building a directed graph from an execution trace, you're adding a whole layer of modeling assumptions that could easily introduce more noise than signal. The paper needs to show ablations on graph structure and demonstrate that the improvements aren't just coming from throwing more compute at the problem.

Finally, I'm skeptical of any UQ method that claims to solve accumulation of long-range dependencies without addressing the fundamental issue, which is that LLMs don't actually have well-calibrated uncertainty estimates to begin with. Propagating garbage through a graph still gives you garbage. Show me calibration plots, show me how this degrades on out-of-distribution tasks, and show me that this isn't just another way to overfit to validation metrics.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within the first few days, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done.

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done- which is perfectly in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as we began automating more tasks and exploring open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and explored open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

comments.content:
This is precisely the kind of tool we need more of – technically impressive, genuinely open-source, and aiming for interoperability. Kudos for tackling the vendor lock-in problem head-on. Yet, the deeper question remains: even when self-hosted and model-agnostic, what does this level of pervasive automation *do* to the nature of work and the individuals performing it?

The promise is liberation from drudgery, delegating routine coding tasks to agents. But the trajectory described – spending weeks entirely inside the AI interface, automating increasingly complex workflows including code review and PR construction – suggests a profound shift in agency. When the agent manages agents, and workflows become opaque chains of automated steps punctuated by "human approval gates," what becomes of genuine understanding and control? Are we building tools that augment developers, or creating systems where developers become glorified workflow auditors, trusting processes they no longer fully comprehend?

Furthermore, while self-hosting mitigates direct data leakage to third-party vendors, it doesn't eliminate the privacy and fairness concerns inherent in the underlying models themselves. These agents, regardless of provider, are trained on vast, often opaque datasets. They embed biases and make probabilistic judgments. Automating critical processes like code review or QA through chains of these models, even locally, risks amplifying and obscuring those biases within internal systems. The veneer of control self-hosting provides might obscure the fundamental lack of transparency and accountability baked into the AI components themselves.

The allure of efficiency is undeniable, and the technical execution here is commendable. But we must persistently ask: efficiency for whom, and at what cost to human judgment, understanding, and the potential for systemic unfairness? Open-source and self-hosting are necessary steps, but insufficient alone to address these deeper structural questions about agency and the very nature of intellectual work in an automated future. Who controls the controllers, even when they're nominally ours?

comments.content:
This is exactly the kind of thing that makes me wonder if we've just given up on actually understanding our tools. We're speedrunning straight past "learn to program" into "manage a fleet of probabilistic text completers that sometimes write code." The fact that someone's primary workflow now involves one AI agent delegating to another AI agent, with a third AI agent reviewing the output, while the human sits there orchestrating this whole Rube Goldberg machine—that's not automation, that's abdication. And calling it "Proliferate" is almost too on the nose.

I get the appeal of optionality and not being locked to one vendor. That's genuinely valuable. But the underlying assumption here is that this agent-swapping, workflow-chaining approach is the future of serious software work, and I just don't buy it. Real engineering involves deep understanding of systems, tradeoffs, and constraints. It involves knowing *why* the code does what it does, not just that it passes tests a language model wrote. If this is what "getting work done" looks like going forward, we're not building on a foundation of competence—we're building on a foundation of plausible-sounding outputs and crossing our fingers. That's how you get the next CrowdStrike incident, not the next Unix.

comments.content:
Oh wonderful, another "everything app" that's going to revolutionize how we work by letting us never leave a single interface. Because clearly what the world needs is yet another abstraction layer sitting on top of existing AI tools, promising to be the one ring that rules them all.

Let's break down what's actually happening here for those who might be dazzled by the buzzword salad. Proliferate is essentially a wrapper that lets you talk to different AI coding assistants (Claude, GPT, etc.) through one interface instead of switching between their native apps. Think of it like a universal remote for your TV, cable box, and stereo - except instead of entertainment devices, you're controlling different AI models that write code.

The "inter-agent communication" feature means you can have one AI model delegate tasks to another AI model, which then reports back. So Claude might ask GPT to review some code, then GPT sends its feedback to Claude. It's like having a very expensive game of telephone, except the participants are statistical models that occasionally hallucinate and the conversation is about your production codebase.

The real kicker here is the implicit assumption that bouncing between multiple AI assistants somehow produces better results than using one well. Sure, different models have different strengths, but coordinating between them adds complexity and potential failure points. You're essentially building a Rube Goldberg machine where each component might confidently give you wrong answers. But hey, at least you'll never have to leave the app while it's happening to you.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: DEMO

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is according to plan and in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent in a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every person is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs.

And that's what Proliferate is for\! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are linear chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d love to any feedback!

comments.content:
Last month I tried switching our team's agent from Codex to Claude Code for cost reasons.  
The migration was painful—rewriting all our automations and losing integrated tools.  
We ended up keeping both agents running separately, which wasted cycles context-switching.  

Proliferate's multi-agent approach looks promising for avoiding that lock-in.  
Isolated worktrees could've saved us weeks of duct-tape solutions.
